technical.definition: Medical diagnostic equipment that uses X-ray beams rotating around the body to generate cross-sectional images through computer processing.
technical.why: Covers emergency, cardiovascular, oncology and routine exams; procurement should consider slice count, gantry aperture, dose control, workflow and service.
technical.choose: Select slice count by clinical needs and budget; for cardiac/emergency, ≥128-slice is recommended; consider mobile/portable options for space-limited sites; compare service terms and lifecycle costs.
technical.mistakes: Focusing only on slice count while ignoring service and site build costs; overlooking dose-quality balance; ignoring accessories and training.

technical.definition: Diagnostic technology that uses strong magnetic fields and radio frequency pulses to excite hydrogen atoms in the body, generating high-resolution images by detecting signal changes.
technical.why: Superior soft-tissue contrast for neuro, MSK and oncology; procurement should consider field strength, coil ecosystem, acoustic quietness and service response.
technical.choose: Choose between 1.5T and 3T based on specialty needs; prioritize quiet technologies, patient comfort and high-channel coils; verify parts coverage and service SLAs.
technical.mistakes: Overemphasizing field strength while ignoring coil ecosystem and service quality; overlooking shielding and site requirements; neglecting workflow and training.

technical.definition: The thickness of each tomographic image in a CT scan, usually in millimeters (mm). Thinner slices mean higher resolution but increased scan time.
technical.why: Directly affects spatial resolution and noise, critical for bone detail and small lesion visibility.
technical.choose: Prefer thin slices for bone/high-detail tasks; in low-dose or fast scans, balance slice thickness with reconstruction kernels and noise.
technical.mistakes: Pursuing ultra-thin slices without considering noise and artifacts; ignoring patient dose and total exam time impacts.

technical.definition: The intensity of the magnetic field produced by MRI equipment, measured in Tesla (T). Common strengths are 1.5T, 3.0T, and 7.0T; higher strength generally means better image quality.
technical.why: Directly affects SNR and contrast performance; higher fields benefit research and high-resolution tasks.
technical.choose: Balance budget and specialty needs between 1.5T and 3.0T; consider quiet technologies and wide-bore designs for comfort.
technical.mistakes: Focusing solely on field strength while ignoring gradient/RF systems and coil ecosystem; underestimating shielding and operations.

technical.definition: Magnet and gradient field containment strategies, commonly active shielding plus EMI control, to reduce fringe fields and site requirements.
Improving magnetic field homogeneity (DSV) via passive/active coils or algorithms to enhance image quality and sequence stability.
The minimum diameter of the patient bore (e.g., 60 cm), affecting comfort, positioning, and coil compatibility.
Helium evaporation and refill requirements under normal operation; “zero consumption” indicates sealed/zero boil-off designs.
Maximum helium capacity in the magnet (e.g., ≤1300 L), related to cryogenic stability and maintenance.
The safety boundary where field strength reaches 5 gauss, used for site planning and safety control.
Total magnet weight including helium and operational state weight, affecting load bearing and logistics.
Maximum RF transmit power under various sequences, linked to patient SAR and sequence availability.
System control and stability of center frequency (e.g., ≤0.07 Hz), impacting sequence consistency and artifact control.
Maximum RF transmit bandwidth under various sequences (e.g., ≤550 kHz), affecting contrast, selectivity and sequence robustness.
technical.why: Controls pulse selectivity and performance; critical for sequence stability and contrast control.
technical.choose: Narrow bandwidth improves selectivity; wider bandwidth enhances pulse robustness; optimize by sequence and target tissue.
technical.mistakes: Ignoring trade-offs among bandwidth, chemical shift and selectivity; overlooking hardware limits.

technical.definition: Per-channel receive bandwidth capability (e.g., ≥1 MHz), affecting chemical shift artifacts and sampling performance.
technical.why: Determines sampling rate and chemical shift control; core to frequency-domain imaging stability.
technical.choose: Higher bandwidth reduces chemical shift/distortion but raises noise; balance with resolution and timing.
technical.mistakes: Blindly increasing bandwidth raises noise; ignoring sequence/coil constraints on bandwidth.

technical.definition: Maximum number of parallel receive channels, affecting parallel imaging acceleration and coil combination flexibility.
Maximum number of coil interfaces, determining how many coils can be connected simultaneously and layout options.
Maximum single-axis gradient strength (e.g., ≥33 mT/m), affecting minimum slice thickness, resolution, and advanced sequence capabilities.
technical.why: Determines spatial resolution and fast sequence capability; a core indicator for advanced body and neuro protocols.
technical.choose: Evaluate together with slew rate; prioritize higher Gmax and robust cooling for advanced tasks.
technical.mistakes: Ignoring continuous performance and thermal management; overlooking practical sequence availability and artifact control.

technical.definition: Rate of gradient change (e.g., ≥100 mT/m/ms), impacting fast sequences and EPI performance and artifact control.
technical.why: Impacts temporal resolution and artifact control in fast sequences, critical for EPI/functional imaging.
technical.choose: Assess with Gmax; focus on stability and cooling under high load.
technical.mistakes: Overlooking patient comfort and acoustic noise; not evaluating derating and temperature rise in continuous scans.

technical.definition: Thermal management schemes for RF amplifiers and gradient systems (e.g., water cooling), affecting stability and continuous operation.
Spatial coverage of imaging (minimum/maximum FOV), affecting resolution, distortion, and clinical applicability.
Time interval between two excitations, influencing contrast and SNR; a core sequence parameter.
Time point of signal sampling, influencing contrast and sensitivity; works with TR to determine image characteristics.
Reconstruction matrix size (e.g., 256×256, 512×512), affecting spatial resolution, acquisition time and noise behavior.
technical.why: Larger matrix increases detail but requires higher SNR and longer time; closely tied to FOV/pixel size.
technical.choose: Increase matrix for high-detail tasks; balance with bandwidth, acceleration factor and coil channels.
technical.mistakes: Blindly increasing matrix raises noise and time; ignoring FOV and patient size constraints.

technical.definition: Acceleration technique using multi-channel coils (factors e.g., ≥2/4/8) to reduce time and artifacts while maintaining resolution.
technical.why: Significantly reduces acquisition time in time-sensitive tasks, lowering motion artifacts and wait time.
technical.choose: Decide factor by coil channels and SNR; beware residual artifacts and noise amplification at high R.
technical.mistakes: Excessive acceleration causes reconstruction artifacts and notable SNR loss; ignoring coil geometry and sensitivity calibration.

technical.definition: Lowering scan acoustic noise via hardware silencing and sequence optimization, improving patient comfort and compliance.
Prospective/retrospective techniques to suppress motion artifacts, applicable to multiple regions and contrasts.
Rapid 3D imaging based on chemical shift to separate water/fat, commonly used in abdominal and body imaging.
CT gantry opening diameter (e.g., ≥80 cm), affecting positioning and accommodation of large patients.
Time for the gantry to complete a 360° rotation (e.g., ≤0.28 s), impacting temporal resolution and cardiac imaging.
technical.why: Directly determines temporal resolution; essential for cardiac and rapid imaging scenarios.
technical.choose: Prefer shorter rotation time for cardiac tasks; balance gantry stability and dose control.
technical.mistakes: Chasing extreme specs while ignoring image quality and noise; overlooking workflow impact on actual speed.

technical.definition: System ability to resolve rapid motion (e.g., ≤30 ms), crucial for cardiac and dynamic imaging.
X-ray tube focal size (e.g., 1.2×0.7 mm), affecting spatial resolution and heat load management.
technical.why: Smaller focal spots improve spatial resolution but reduce heat handling; balance by task intensity.
technical.choose: Prefer small focal spots for bone/high-detail tasks; for continuous high-load scans, consider larger focal spots.
technical.mistakes: Focusing only on small focal spots while ignoring heat capacity and continuity; overlooking reconstruction kernel and noise.

technical.definition: Maximum heat the tube anode can withstand (e.g., ≥6.8 MHu), determining continuous scan and high-load capability.
technical.why: Determines stability and downtime risk under prolonged and high-load scanning.
technical.choose: Prioritize higher capacity for cardiac and large coverage tasks; evaluate together with cooling rate.
technical.mistakes: Ignoring sustained load and cooling ability; underestimating efficiency loss from cooldown downtime.

technical.definition: Heat the tube can dissipate per unit time (e.g., ≥2.0 MHu/min), affecting workflow efficiency and overheat protection.
technical.why: Determines turnaround efficiency and stability under high workload.
technical.choose: Favor higher cooling rate in high-throughput scenarios; consider whole‑system cooling and room HVAC.
technical.mistakes: Ignoring overall cooling bottlenecks and environment; not assessing derating strategy for continuous scans.

technical.definition: Tube current range during scanning (e.g., 10–700 mA), influencing dose and image noise.
technical.why: Directly impacts dose and noise; core variable for dose management and image quality.
technical.choose: Configure by body habitus and region; pair with AEC and iterative reconstruction to balance dose and quality.
technical.mistakes: Increasing mA blindly without dose control; ignoring reconstruction and kernel impact on quality.

technical.definition: Tube accelerating voltage range (e.g., 80–140 kVp), affecting contrast, penetration and spectral imaging performance.
technical.why: Impacts material contrast and dose efficiency; key parameter for spectral and dose optimization.
technical.choose: Use lower kVp for pediatrics/low-dose; for iodine-enhanced exams, tailor kVp with mA to body habitus.
technical.mistakes: Using fixed kVp without considering task/body habitus; not leveraging spectral strategies to boost contrast.

technical.definition: Display and reconstruction matrix dimensions (e.g., 512×512, 1024×1024), affecting resolution and post-processing.
technical.why: Larger matrices add detail but demand higher sampling and raise noise; increase compute load.
technical.choose: Increase matrix for high-detail tasks; coordinate with FOV, pixel size and reconstruction kernel.
technical.mistakes: Blindly enlarging matrix increases pixel noise; ignoring FOV and sampling physical limits.

technical.definition: Supported non-extended CT value range (e.g., −1024 to 3072 HU), used for tissue density quantification.
Physical number of detector rows along the Z-axis (e.g., ≥128 rows), determining coverage and scanning speed.
Number of imaging layers in the detector direction (e.g., ≥256 layers), affecting equivalent resolution and reconstruction capability.
CT Data Acquisition System sampling frequency per second (e.g., ≥8900 Hz), impacting temporal resolution and high‑speed scans.
Gantry slip ring data transfer rate (e.g., ≥20 Gbps), ensuring stable links under high‑speed rotation.
Geometric distance from tube focal spot to detector (e.g., ≤110 cm), affecting magnification, scatter, and spatial resolution.
Distance from tube focal spot to the center of the scan field (e.g., ≥62 cm), influencing projection geometry and parameter setup.
Acoustic noise at maximum rotation speed (e.g., ≤69 dB), related to patient comfort and compliance.
Physical element count per detector row (e.g., ≥830), impacting sampling density and spatial resolution.
Total number of detector elements per single layer (e.g., ≥106000), determining coverage and image detail.
Upper limit of system dynamic range (e.g., ≥160 dB), determining measurability and linearity across weak/strong signals.
Spatial resolution metric at 10% modulation transfer function in planar directions, indicating fine detail performance.
Composite contrast/detail performance metric at 50% MTF in planar directions.
Resolution metric along slice direction, reflecting volumetric coverage and layer detail.
Contrast/detail metric along slice direction, commonly used in phantom evaluations.
Ability to detect low‑contrast targets under specified phantom and CTDIvol conditions (e.g., 5 mm @ 0.3%).
Geometric pitch range for helical scans (e.g., ≥0.508:1–1.5:1), affecting speed, coverage, and artifacts.
Physical Z‑axis collimation coverage per rotation (e.g., ≥8 cm), determining volumetric efficiency.
Maximum uninterrupted helical scan duration (e.g., ≥60 s), reflecting thermal and stability capacity.
Time delay from threshold/gating trigger to scan start (e.g., ≤1 s), impacting timing alignment and cardiac protocols.
Maximum geometric coverage of the scan field (e.g., ≥50 cm), impacting large body habitus and whole‑body coverage.
Maximum field of view for display/post‑processing (e.g., ≥50 cm), related to matrix and FOV configuration.
Matrix dimension of the display pipeline (e.g., ≥1024×1024), complements reconstruction matrix for visual detail.
CT dose index per unit volume, reflecting protocol radiation level for dose management and comparisons.
Total dose across the entire exam proportional to scan length.
Strategy to automatically modulate tube current based on anatomy/thickness to optimize dose and image quality.
mA modulation across cardiac cycle to boost key phases and reduce dose in non‑key phases.
Iterative reconstruction using optics/noise/physics models to significantly reduce noise and improve low‑contrast detection.
Relative dose reduction percentage versus filtering/FBP under specified algorithms and phantoms (e.g., ≥82%).
Regulatory status for a specific technology/algorithm (e.g., FDA/NMPA), reflecting compliance and trustworthiness.
Quantitative measurement and parametric maps of tissue T1 values for myocardium and multi‑system assessment.
Quantitative measurement of tissue T2 reflecting hydration and inflammatory processes.
Quantification related to R2* dephasing effects, used for iron deposition and microbleed analysis.
Estimated interstitial volume fraction via T1 mapping and hematocrit, used for myocardial fibrosis assessment.
Quantitative parameter from diffusion‑weighted imaging reflecting restricted diffusion; used in oncology and stroke.
DTI metric reflecting integrity and directionality of white matter fiber structures.
Quantitative parameter related to T2* for iron deposition and oxygenation changes.
Quantitative parameter in the rotating frame reflecting biochemical changes and viscosity in cartilage.
Quantitative parameter derived from magnetization transfer effects to assess myelin and tissue composition changes.
Plasma–interstitium transfer constant in DCE quantification, reflecting permeability and perfusion properties.
Number of image layers acquired per rotation in axial mode (e.g., ≥256), impacting coverage and efficiency.
Z‑axis coverage per rotation in axial scans (e.g., ≥8 cm), reflecting volumetric efficiency per acquisition.
Detector Z coverage per rotation in cine scans (e.g., ≥8 cm), for dynamic or high frame‑rate scenarios.
High‑definition scan modes supported (axial, helical, cine) to optimize detail and temporal performance across scenarios.
Time to switch from axial to helical (e.g., ≤3 s), reflecting workflow responsiveness.
Number of available gantry control panels (e.g., ≥4), affecting convenience and redundancy.
Built‑in patient information display on the gantry for identity confirmation and operator guidance.
Post collimator structure blocking scatter in X/Y/Z and guiding incident X‑rays precisely to reduce artifacts and improve quality.
Combined post‑collimator and algorithmic strategies to suppress beam hardening and metal artifacts for clinical readability.
Quantitative imaging of metabolites and chemical environment; commonly used for oncology and metabolic assessment.
Vascular imaging without contrast agent (e.g., 4D NCEMRA) for vessel assessment and follow‑up.
Contrast‑based vascular imaging (e.g., 4D CEMRA) to improve visualization and quantitative evaluation.

performance.definition: The minimum distance between two adjacent structures that an imaging system can distinguish, determining image clarity and detail display capability.
The ability of an imaging system to distinguish tissues of different densities or signal intensities, especially important for soft tissue imaging.
The time required to complete a full scan, affecting patient comfort and equipment efficiency.
Random signals in the image caused by system electronic noise, quantum noise, etc., affecting image quality.

clinical.definition: Drugs injected into the body to enhance the visibility of specific tissues or blood vessels, improving lesion detection rates and diagnostic accuracy.
Imaging technology that not only shows tissue structure but also reflects organ functional status, such as functional MRI, perfusion imaging, etc.
Post-processing technology that reconstructs cross-sectional images into coronal, sagittal, or arbitrary angle planes.
The amount of ionizing radiation a patient receives during an X-ray examination, measured in millisieverts (mSv), which needs to be strictly controlled.
CT imaging using energy spectrum decomposition to differentiate materials and contrasts; supports volumetry and gout/stone analysis.
CT architecture with two tube/detector chains, improving temporal resolution and motion robustness for cardiac imaging.
Timing cardiac CT/MRI acquisitions using ECG trigger or phase selection to optimize temporal alignment and dose.
Non-contrast perfusion MRI by magnetizing inflowing blood; widely used for cerebral perfusion assessment.
Time-series contrast acquisition and quantitative analysis for perfusion, permeability, and microenvironment evaluation.
Functional imaging based on blood oxygen level–dependent signal changes for brain activation and network mapping.
Advanced diffusion techniques for anisotropy quantification and white matter fiber tractography.
Multi‑b value fitting to separate perfusion and diffusion components for microcirculation evaluation.
Assessing non‑Gaussian diffusion behavior to reflect tissue complexity and microstructural changes.
Quantitative imaging via susceptibility inversion for metals, iron deposition, and oxygenation‑related changes.
Molecular imaging technique using selective saturation to visualize metabolites and chemical environments.
Capturing signals from very short‑T2 tissues (e.g., cortical bone, lung) using extremely short TE for structure and quantification.
3D dynamic quantification of blood flow velocity and direction for cardiovascular assessment.
Sparse reconstruction‑based acceleration enabling faster 2D/3D/4D sequences while maintaining resolution.
Non‑contrast MRA leveraging unsaturated inflowing blood signal entering the imaging volume for vessel visualization.
Vascular imaging based on phase changes to quantify blood flow velocity and direction.
Suppresses intraluminal blood signal to highlight vessel wall and myocardial structures; useful for plaque and inflammation assessment.
Delayed‑phase myocardial imaging after contrast injection to assess fibrosis, scar, and ischemia/infarction.
Cine acquisition under free breathing with motion correction/navigation to improve patient compliance.
CT examination for coronary artery evaluation including stenosis, plaque, and anatomical variants.
Spectral reconstruction of single‑energy images at various keV to reduce noise, suppress metal artifacts, and optimize contrast.
Equivalent atomic number derived from spectral material decomposition for identification and quantitative analysis.
Quantification of iodine concentration (mg/ml) via spectral imaging for perfusion, enhancement, and lesion analysis.
Reconstruction strategy using trained deep networks for denoising and detail recovery, improving low‑dose image quality.
Structured dose report in DICOM for compliance and tracking of exam dose metrics.
Tube current modulation strategy targeting sensitive organs to reduce localized radiation.
Acquisition within predefined ECG phase windows; lower dose but limited phase range, suitable for stable heart rates.
Continuous acquisition with phase selection during post‑processing; flexible temporal resolution but higher dose, for unstable heart rates.
Ratio of image signal to noise that drives readability and detail rendering.
Contrast between tissues relative to noise, a stronger indicator of clinical interpretability.
Quantitative assessment and correction of main magnetic field inhomogeneity to reduce distortion and stabilize sequences.
Measurement and correction of RF field inhomogeneity to improve contrast and quantitative accuracy.
Mainstream parallel imaging reconstruction methods leveraging multi‑channel coils for acceleration while maintaining resolution.
High‑SNR sequence commonly used for rapid cardiac/body imaging; sensitive to B0/B1 but offers strong contrast and temporal performance.
Ultra‑fast acquisition widely used for DWI/BOLD, but prone to distortion and susceptibility artifacts.
